fixes.explanation: That's exactly what Abimelech says: "God is with you in all that you do." (Genesis 21:22) Abimelech, king of Gerar (Genesis 20:2), says it together with Phicol, the commander of his army. They could have opened with anything. They led with God. Nobody is complimenting Abraham's cookie recipe here, friend.

Harshly sounds close, but it's not the word. Abimelech asks Abraham to swear that he will not "deal falsely" with him or his children or descendants. (Genesis 21:23) The oath is about dealing honestly, not about being rough. Good guess, though, friend.
True! Abraham answers, "I swear it." (Genesis 21:24) That's all he says. Three words, and the oath is agreed. I wish my answers to "what do you want for dinner" were that short.

That's it. Abraham complained to Abimelech "…about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized…" (Genesis 21:25) The servants took it, and Abraham brought it straight to the king. I'd guard a well like I guard the last chocolate chip in the bowl.

That would be quite a complaint, friend, but it's not in the text. Abraham complained about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized. (Genesis 21:25) No fire and no burned field. Just a well, and a complaint brought to the king.

Right. Abimelech says, "I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today." (Genesis 21:26) Notice he says two things: he doesn't know who did it, and Abraham hadn't told him. That's a lot of "I don't know" packed into one answer.

Yes! Abraham gave Abimelech sheep and cattle, "…and the two men made a covenant." (Genesis 21:27) A covenant is a solemn agreement between two parties. The text puts the gift and the covenant side by side in one verse. I'd say that beats a handshake and a smile.

Exactly. Abraham says, "You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well." (Genesis 21:30) The lambs stand as his witness. Abimelech asked why they were set apart, and Abraham gave him a clear answer. That's a good habit for any of us.

Yes, Beersheba. The text says the place "…was called Beersheba, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath." (Genesis 21:31) The name comes from what happened right there. Mine got carved into my handle by the family who bought me for a quarter, so I'm a little jealous.

Bethel is a place in Abraham's story, but it's not this one. Genesis 12:8 mentions it earlier, when Abram pitches his tent with Bethel on the west. The place where the two men swore their oath "…was called Beersheba…" (Genesis 21:31) Close, but Bethel will have to wait.

Hebron comes up in Abraham's story too. Genesis 13:18 says he settled by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron. But it's not the answer here. The text says the place where the two swore an oath "…was called Beersheba…" (Genesis 21:31) You're thinking along the right trail, friend.

True. "After they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army got up and returned to the land of the Philistines." (Genesis 21:32) The covenant comes first, and then they go. The very next verse has Abraham planting a tamarisk tree at Beersheba. (Genesis 21:33) So the story keeps going, friend.

Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:15), so I see why she came to mind. But the text never says Abraham builds a house for her here. It says he planted a tamarisk tree, "…and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God." (Genesis 21:33) The tree and the prayer are what happen at Beersheba.

Another well is a fair guess, since a well is what this whole passage keeps coming back to. But the text doesn't say that. It says Abraham planted a tamarisk tree, "…and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God." (Genesis 21:33) No new well is mentioned, friend.
